examTakeaway: A postmenopausal woman under 65 without increased fracture risk is not offered routine bone-density screening.
scenario: A 52-year-old woman is two years past menopause. She has no fracture, no parent with a hip fracture, no smoking, no steroid use, and a normal weight. A colleague orders routine densitometry because menopause itself is the indication.
question: Does menopause alone at age 52 justify routine screening?
options: No. Under 65, routine screening is for increased risk, which she does not have
Yes. Every woman is screened from the day of menopause
Yes, and treatment starts before the result returns
No woman is ever screened, including after 65
A hip x-ray replaces densitometry at this age
correctAnswer: No. Under 65, routine screening is for increased risk, which she does not have
explanation:
A postmenopausal woman under 65 without increased fracture risk is not offered routine bone-density screening. Menopause alone is not that risk list. She has none of the factors that would move the test earlier. US Preventive Services Task Force osteoporosis screening recommendation, 2025.

No. Under 65, routine screening is for increased risk, which she does not have
Yes. Every woman is screened from the day of menopause — The universal age is 65. Earlier testing needs increased risk.
Yes, and treatment starts before the result returns — There is no result, and there is no fracture to treat blindly.
No woman is ever screened, including after 65 — Screening at 65 and older is recommended. She is simply younger and low risk.
A hip x-ray replaces densitometry at this age — A plain film is not the screening test.
citation: US Preventive Services Task Force osteoporosis screening recommendation, 2025.

examTakeaway: A hip fracture from a fall is enough to start osteoporosis treatment. Densitometry is not a reason to delay the drug.
scenario: A 74-year-old woman broke her hip in a fall from standing. The fracture is fixed. She has never had a bone-density test. A colleague says no osteoporosis drug can start until that scan is done next month.
question: Does the missing scan delay treatment?
options: Yes. No drug is allowed until a T-score returns
No. The hip fracture from standing height is already the indication to treat
Calcium alone for a year and no antiresorptive drug
A week of high-dose prednisone to strengthen the bone
Treatment only if a second hip fractures
correctAnswer: No. The hip fracture from standing height is already the indication to treat
explanation:
A hip fracture from a fall is enough to start osteoporosis treatment. Densitometry is not a reason to delay the drug. She can still be scanned, but the drug does not wait a month for the picture. Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on pharmacological management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women, 2019.

No. The hip fracture from standing height is already the indication to treat
Yes. No drug is allowed until a T-score returns — The fracture is the indication. The scan is not a gate.
Calcium alone for a year and no antiresorptive drug — Calcium does not replace treatment after a hip fracture.
A week of high-dose prednisone to strengthen the bone — A steroid week weakens bone. It is not the treatment.
Treatment only if a second hip fractures — The first fragility hip fracture is enough.
citation: Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline on pharmacological management of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women, 2019.

examTakeaway: Axial spondyloarthritis starts with an NSAID trial. A TNF inhibitor is not the first prescription when an NSAID has not been tried.
scenario: A 27-year-old man has inflammatory back pain for 8 months, worse at night and better with activity. His HLA-B27 is positive and his CRP is high. He has never taken an NSAID. A colleague starts a TNF inhibitor and says NSAIDs are obsolete.
question: What is tried before the TNF inhibitor?
options: A TNF inhibitor immediately, with no NSAID
Long-term opioids for night pain
A full NSAID trial, because he has not had one
Antibiotics for presumed infection of the sacroiliac joint
Bed rest until the CRP normalizes
correctAnswer: A full NSAID trial, because he has not had one
explanation:
Axial spondyloarthritis starts with an NSAID trial. A TNF inhibitor is not the first prescription when an NSAID has not been tried. His diagnosis can be right and the first drug can still be an NSAID. 2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN recommendations for the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis.

A full NSAID trial, because he has not had one
A TNF inhibitor immediately, with no NSAID — The biologic is not the first drug in a patient who has never tried an NSAID.
Long-term opioids for night pain — Opioids are not the disease treatment.
Antibiotics for presumed infection of the sacroiliac joint — Eight months of inflammatory pain with this pattern is not treated as acute septic arthritis.
Bed rest until the CRP normalizes — Activity is part of care. Rest until the CRP falls is not the plan.
citation: 2019 ACR/SAA/SPARTAN recommendations for the treatment of ankylosing spondylitis and nonradiographic axial spondyloarthritis.

examTakeaway: Newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia with platelets under 30,000 is treated with a corticosteroid. A count of 18,000 is already under that line.
scenario: A 32-year-old woman has petechiae and a platelet count of 18,000 per microliter. Hemoglobin is 13 g/dL, the blood film shows no schistocytes, and she is not pregnant. A colleague observes her for a month because she is not bleeding from the mouth.
question: Does a count of 18,000 without mouth bleeding still get treatment?
options: No. Treatment waits for oral wet purpura or a count under 5,000
Platelet transfusion as the only therapy
Heparin, because a low platelet count is always a clotting problem
Yes. A corticosteroid is started because the count is under 30,000
Aspirin to improve the petechiae
correctAnswer: Yes. A corticosteroid is started because the count is under 30,000
explanation:
Newly diagnosed immune thrombocytopenia with platelets under 30,000 is treated with a corticosteroid. A count of 18,000 is already under that line. Mouth bleeding is not required. Observation is for higher counts without bleeding. ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

Yes. A corticosteroid is started because the count is under 30,000
No. Treatment waits for oral wet purpura or a count under 5,000 — The threshold to treat newly diagnosed disease is 30,000, not 5,000.
Platelet transfusion as the only therapy — Transfusion is for serious bleeding, not the routine treatment of this count.
Heparin, because a low platelet count is always a clotting problem — Heparin is not the treatment, and this film is not a microangiopathy.
Aspirin to improve the petechiae — Aspirin worsens bleeding. It is not used here.
citation: ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Immune thrombocytopenia with platelets of 50,000 and no bleeding is observed. Steroids are not mandatory at that count.
scenario: A 40-year-old man has a platelet count of 50,000 found on a routine panel. He has no petechiae, no wet purpura, and no planned surgery. Hemoglobin and leukocytes are normal. A colleague starts high-dose dexamethasone because any count under 100,000 is treated.
question: Is treatment required at 50,000 with no bleeding?
options: Yes. Every count under 100,000 starts dexamethasone
Yes, with platelet transfusion until the count exceeds 150,000
Yes, with aspirin so the platelets that remain work harder
No treatment is ever given, even under 10,000
No. Observation is appropriate above 30,000 when there is no bleeding
correctAnswer: No. Observation is appropriate above 30,000 when there is no bleeding
explanation:
Immune thrombocytopenia with platelets of 50,000 and no bleeding is observed. Steroids are not mandatory at that count. A threshold of 100,000 is not the rule. He has no procedure that needs a higher count. ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

No. Observation is appropriate above 30,000 when there is no bleeding
Yes. Every count under 100,000 starts dexamethasone — The usual treatment line for newly diagnosed disease is under 30,000 or bleeding.
Yes, with platelet transfusion until the count exceeds 150,000 — Transfusion is not used to chase a normal number.
Yes, with aspirin so the platelets that remain work harder — Aspirin is not a treatment for a low platelet count.
No treatment is ever given, even under 10,000 — Very low counts are treated. His count is simply not in that range.
citation: ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia means all heparin stops and a non-heparin anticoagulant starts. Warfarin is not started alone while the platelet count is low.
scenario: A 68-year-old woman was on unfractionated heparin for 8 days. Her platelets fell from 220,000 to 70,000. One leg is newly swollen. The 4T score is high. A colleague stops heparin and starts warfarin alone that evening.
question: What replaces the heparin?
options: A non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, not warfarin by itself
Warfarin alone on the evening heparin stops
Platelet transfusion to 100,000 and continued heparin
Observation until an antibody returns, with no anticoagulant
Low-molecular-weight heparin as a safe substitute
correctAnswer: A non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, not warfarin by itself
explanation:
Suspected heparin-induced thrombocytopenia means all heparin stops and a non-heparin anticoagulant starts. Warfarin is not started alone while the platelet count is low. She already has a high score and a swollen leg. Warfarin alone risks limb gangrene while the count is 70,000. ASH 2018 guidelines for management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

A non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban, not warfarin by itself
Warfarin alone on the evening heparin stops — Warfarin monotherapy during the low count is the error.
Platelet transfusion to 100,000 and continued heparin — Platelets are not given for the count alone, and heparin is not continued.
Observation until an antibody returns, with no anticoagulant — A high score with thrombosis is not observed off anticoagulation.
Low-molecular-weight heparin as a safe substitute — Every heparin product stops. A low-molecular-weight product is still heparin.
citation: ASH 2018 guidelines for management of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Stable neutropenic fever starts with one antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Vancomycin is not automatic.
scenario: A 60-year-old man on chemotherapy has a temperature of 38.6 C. His neutrophil count is 200 per microliter. Blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg, he has no line redness, and there is no hemodynamic instability. A colleague adds vancomycin to cefepime because every neutropenic fever includes MRSA coverage.
question: Is vancomycin part of the initial regimen?
options: Yes. Vancomycin is required in every neutropenic fever
No. Cefepime alone is enough while he is stable and the line looks normal
No antibiotic until a culture grows
Vancomycin alone, without the beta-lactam
Hold antibiotics unless the temperature exceeds 40 C
correctAnswer: No. Cefepime alone is enough while he is stable and the line looks normal
explanation:
Stable neutropenic fever starts with one antipseudomonal beta-lactam. Vancomycin is not automatic. He is not unstable and the line is not red. Adding vancomycin is the habit the guideline rejects. ASCO/IDSA 2018 guideline on fever and neutropenia: routine vancomycin is not part of the initial regimen for a stable patient.

No. Cefepime alone is enough while he is stable and the line looks normal
Yes. Vancomycin is required in every neutropenic fever — Routine addition is not the initial regimen.
No antibiotic until a culture grows — Fever and neutropenia are treated immediately. The culture does not have to grow first.
Vancomycin alone, without the beta-lactam — Vancomycin does not cover Pseudomonas. The beta-lactam is the required drug.
Hold antibiotics unless the temperature exceeds 40 C — 38.6 C with neutropenia is already the indication.
citation: ASCO/IDSA 2018 guideline on fever and neutropenia: routine vancomycin is not part of the initial regimen for a stable patient.

examTakeaway: Vancomycin is added to neutropenic fever when the patient is unstable or a catheter infection is suspected, not because the temperature exists.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman with neutropenia has a temperature of 38.8 C and a blood pressure of 82/48 mm Hg. Her tunneled line site is red and tender. She is already receiving cefepime. A colleague refuses vancomycin because the first rule said not to use it routinely.
question: Why is vancomycin now the right addition?
options: Vancomycin is never added, even in shock
Stop cefepime and use vancomycin alone
She is in shock and the line looks infected, which are the reasons to add it
Add it only after 96 hours of fever if the pressure is normal
Steroids instead of any change in antibiotics
correctAnswer: She is in shock and the line looks infected, which are the reasons to add it
explanation:
Vancomycin is added to neutropenic fever when the patient is unstable or a catheter infection is suspected, not because the temperature exists. Both of those reasons are present. The routine-vancomycin ban does not apply to this picture. ASCO/IDSA 2018 guideline on fever and neutropenia: routine vancomycin is not part of the initial regimen for a stable patient.

She is in shock and the line looks infected, which are the reasons to add it
Vancomycin is never added, even in shock — Shock and a red line are exactly when it is added.
Stop cefepime and use vancomycin alone — The antipseudomonal drug stays. Vancomycin is added.
Add it only after 96 hours of fever if the pressure is normal — Her pressure is 82/48. Waiting 96 hours is the stable-fever pathway, not this one.
Steroids instead of any change in antibiotics — Steroids do not cover a line infection in shock.
citation: ASCO/IDSA 2018 guideline on fever and neutropenia: routine vancomycin is not part of the initial regimen for a stable patient.

examTakeaway: Platelet transfusion in immune thrombocytopenia is for serious bleeding, not for a low number alone.
scenario: A 29-year-old man with immune thrombocytopenia has a platelet count of 12,000 and scattered petechiae. He is hemodynamically stable, with no intracranial symptom and no gastrointestinal bleeding. A colleague transfuses platelets until the count exceeds 50,000 and holds the corticosteroid.
question: Is transfusion the treatment of this count?
options: Yes. Any count under 20,000 is transfused to 50,000 before a drug
Transfuse and skip the corticosteroid
Aspirin plus transfusion
No. Start a corticosteroid. Transfusion is reserved for serious bleeding, which he does not have
No drug and no transfusion even if intracranial bleeding starts
correctAnswer: No. Start a corticosteroid. Transfusion is reserved for serious bleeding, which he does not have
explanation:
Platelet transfusion in immune thrombocytopenia is for serious bleeding, not for a low number alone. Petechiae are not that bleeding. The disease treatment is a corticosteroid, and transfused platelets are destroyed quickly. ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

No. Start a corticosteroid. Transfusion is reserved for serious bleeding, which he does not have
Yes. Any count under 20,000 is transfused to 50,000 before a drug — The number alone is not a transfusion indication.
Transfuse and skip the corticosteroid — The corticosteroid is the treatment. Transfusion does not replace it.
Aspirin plus transfusion — Aspirin is harmful with this count.
No drug and no transfusion even if intracranial bleeding starts — Serious bleeding would change the plan. He simply does not have it now.
citation: ASH 2019 guidelines for immune thrombocytopenia.

examTakeaway: Severe albuminuria without diabetes is still a reason to start an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Moderate albuminuria without diabetes is not the same automatic start.
scenario: A 58-year-old woman has no diabetes. Her urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 420 mg/g and her estimated filtration rate is 58 mL/min/1.73 m2. Blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg and potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. A colleague withholds an ACE inhibitor because she does not have diabetes.
question: Does the missing diabetes diagnosis remove the ACE inhibitor?
options: Yes. The class is only for diabetic kidney disease
No, so start an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together
Yes, unless the filtration rate is below 15
No drug until the ratio exceeds 2,000
No. A ratio of 420 is severe albuminuria, and that indication does not require diabetes
correctAnswer: No. A ratio of 420 is severe albuminuria, and that indication does not require diabetes
explanation:
Severe albuminuria without diabetes is still a reason to start an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. Moderate albuminuria without diabetes is not the same automatic start. Her ratio is above 300, so it is the severe category. One drug from the class is started, not both. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

No. A ratio of 420 is severe albuminuria, and that indication does not require diabetes
Yes. The class is only for diabetic kidney disease — Severe albuminuria is an indication with or without diabetes.
No, so start an ACE inhibitor and an ARB together — The indication is one drug, not both.
Yes, unless the filtration rate is below 15 — A filtration rate of 58 is not a reason to withhold the drug.
No drug until the ratio exceeds 2,000 — Severe albuminuria begins above 300. Waiting for 2,000 is not the rule.
citation: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

examTakeaway: A rise in creatinine of up to 30 percent after an ACE inhibitor can be accepted. A rise well above 30 percent is reassessed and the drug is reduced or stopped.
scenario: A 64-year-old man started lisinopril two weeks ago for albuminuric kidney disease. Creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL. Potassium is 4.6 mEq/L and he is not volume depleted. A colleague calls a 60 percent rise acceptable because any rise under a doubling is ignored.
question: Is a rise from 1.0 to 1.6 mg/dL acceptable?
options: No. That is about a 60 percent rise, which is past the 30 percent limit
Yes. Any rise short of a doubling is ignored
Yes, and the dose should be doubled
No drug in this class can ever change the creatinine
Stop the drug only if potassium exceeds 6
correctAnswer: No. That is about a 60 percent rise, which is past the 30 percent limit
explanation:
A rise in creatinine of up to 30 percent after an ACE inhibitor can be accepted. A rise well above 30 percent is reassessed and the drug is reduced or stopped. From 1.0 to 1.6 is not a small hemodynamic change. Volume status is already adequate, so the dose is not simply continued. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

No. That is about a 60 percent rise, which is past the 30 percent limit
Yes. Any rise short of a doubling is ignored — The accepted rise is about 30 percent, not a near-doubling.
Yes, and the dose should be doubled — A large rise is a reason to reduce the drug, not to increase it.
No drug in this class can ever change the creatinine — A small rise is expected. The error is treating 60 percent as if it were that small rise.
Stop the drug only if potassium exceeds 6 — The creatinine rise is its own reason. The potassium does not have to be 6.
citation: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

examTakeaway: A creatinine rise of about 20 percent after an ACE inhibitor is the expected hemodynamic change and is not a reason to stop the drug.
scenario: A 57-year-old woman started an ACE inhibitor for diabetic albuminuria. Her creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.2 mg/dL. Potassium is 4.5 mEq/L and blood pressure is 124/72 mm Hg. A colleague stops the drug because any rise means acute kidney injury.
question: What should happen to the ACE inhibitor after this rise?
options: Stop it. Any rise is tubular necrosis
Continue it. A rise from 1.0 to 1.2 is within the accepted range
Add a second ACE inhibitor to pull the creatinine back down
Replace it with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug
Continue it only if the creatinine later doubles
correctAnswer: Continue it. A rise from 1.0 to 1.2 is within the accepted range
explanation:
A creatinine rise of about 20 percent after an ACE inhibitor is the expected hemodynamic change and is not a reason to stop the drug. Twenty percent is under 30 percent. Potassium and pressure are acceptable. KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

Continue it. A rise from 1.0 to 1.2 is within the accepted range
Stop it. Any rise is tubular necrosis — A 20 percent rise without illness is the hemodynamic effect, not necrosis.
Add a second ACE inhibitor to pull the creatinine back down — A second drug from the class is not used.
Replace it with a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug — That class worsens kidney perfusion.
Continue it only if the creatinine later doubles — Doubling would be a reason to stop, not the condition for continuing.
citation: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of Chronic Kidney Disease.

examTakeaway: Initial treatment of minimal change disease in adults is high-dose glucocorticoid, not cyclosporine as the first drug.
scenario: A 22-year-old man has sudden edema, urine protein of 6 g per day, and a biopsy that shows minimal change disease. His creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. A colleague starts cyclosporine and says steroids are only for children.
question: Which drug is the initial treatment?
options: Cyclosporine first, because adults do not respond to steroids
An antibiotic for the proteinuria
High-dose glucocorticoid
No drug until the protein exceeds 10 g per day
Immediate dialysis
correctAnswer: High-dose glucocorticoid
explanation:
Initial treatment of minimal change disease in adults is high-dose glucocorticoid, not cyclosporine as the first drug. Adult disease is still treated with steroid first. Cyclosporine is for relapse or steroid failure, which has not happened. KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases.

High-dose glucocorticoid
Cyclosporine first, because adults do not respond to steroids — Adults are treated with glucocorticoid initially.
An antibiotic for the proteinuria — Proteinuria of this pattern is not a bacterial infection.
No drug until the protein exceeds 10 g per day — Six grams with this biopsy is already the indication.
Immediate dialysis — Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Dialysis is not the treatment of minimal change disease.
citation: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases.

examTakeaway: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a nonpregnant adult is not treated. Pregnancy is the setting where screening and treatment apply.
scenario: A 72-year-old woman has no urinary symptoms. A culture collected before an orthopedic visit grows more than 100,000 colonies of E. coli. She is not pregnant. Her temperature is 36.8 C. A colleague prescribes 7 days of an antibiotic because the colony count is high.
question: Does the colony count justify antibiotics?
options: Yes. Any culture above 100,000 colonies is treated
Yes, because age over 70 makes every positive culture a kidney infection
No antibiotic is appropriate for any woman, including in pregnancy
No. Without symptoms and without pregnancy, the culture is not treated
A 14-day intravenous course, because the organism is E. coli
correctAnswer: No. Without symptoms and without pregnancy, the culture is not treated
explanation:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria in a nonpregnant adult is not treated. Pregnancy is the setting where screening and treatment apply. A high colony count does not create symptoms she does not have. US Preventive Services Task Force asymptomatic bacteriuria screening recommendation, 2019.

No. Without symptoms and without pregnancy, the culture is not treated
Yes. Any culture above 100,000 colonies is treated — The colony count is how bacteriuria is defined. It is not, by itself, a treatment indication outside pregnancy.
Yes, because age over 70 makes every positive culture a kidney infection — Age does not convert asymptomatic bacteriuria into pyelonephritis.
No antibiotic is appropriate for any woman, including in pregnancy — Pregnancy is treated. She is not pregnant.
A 14-day intravenous course, because the organism is E. coli — The organism does not change the absence of symptoms.
citation: US Preventive Services Task Force asymptomatic bacteriuria screening recommendation, 2019.

examTakeaway: Uncomplicated cystitis is treated with nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or fosfomycin. A fluoroquinolone is not the first drug.
scenario: A 26-year-old woman has two days of burning and frequency and no fever, no flank pain, and no vomiting. She is not pregnant. A colleague prescribes ciprofloxacin for 7 days and says that drug is first-line for every urinary infection.
question: Which drug class is preferred for this bladder infection?
options: Ciprofloxacin for 7 days as the preferred first drug
No antibiotic, because burning without fever is not infection
Amphotericin, because burning is usually fungal
Nitrofurantoin for one day only
Nitrofurantoin for 5 days, or another recommended cystitis drug, not ciprofloxacin first
correctAnswer: Nitrofurantoin for 5 days, or another recommended cystitis drug, not ciprofloxacin first
explanation:
Uncomplicated cystitis is treated with nitrofurantoin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, or fosfomycin. A fluoroquinolone is not the first drug. She has no fever and no flank pain, so this is cystitis, and ciprofloxacin is reserved. IDSA 2011 guidelines for uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women, which remain the IDSA guidance.

Nitrofurantoin for 5 days, or another recommended cystitis drug, not ciprofloxacin first
Ciprofloxacin for 7 days as the preferred first drug — Fluoroquinolones are not preferred for uncomplicated cystitis.
No antibiotic, because burning without fever is not infection — Cystitis is treated. Fever is not required.
Amphotericin, because burning is usually fungal — Fungal therapy is not the uncomplicated regimen.
Nitrofurantoin for one day only — The nitrofurantoin course is 5 days, not one day.
citation: IDSA 2011 guidelines for uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women, which remain the IDSA guidance.

examTakeaway: Pyelonephritis is not treated with nitrofurantoin. That drug does not reach reliable kidney levels.
scenario: A 30-year-old woman has fever of 38.9 C, flank pain, and vomiting. Her pulse is 110/min and her blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows leukocytes. A colleague prescribes nitrofurantoin for 5 days because that is the cystitis drug.
question: Why is nitrofurantoin the wrong drug for this kidney infection?
options: A drug that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is preferred once the kidney is involved
No antibiotic until a culture grows for 72 hours
Amphotericin as the first drug
A single dose of fosfomycin
correctAnswer: A drug that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin
explanation:
Pyelonephritis is not treated with nitrofurantoin. That drug does not reach reliable kidney levels. Fever, flank pain, and vomiting are not cystitis. The 5-day nitrofurantoin course is the bladder regimen. IDSA 2011 guidelines for uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women, which remain the IDSA guidance.

A drug that reaches kidney tissue, not nitrofurantoin
Nitrofurantoin is preferred once the kidney is involved — Kidney involvement is the reason to stop using it.
No antibiotic until a culture grows for 72 hours — She is febrile and vomiting. Treatment is not delayed three days.
Amphotericin as the first drug — This is a bacterial pyelonephritis pattern, not a fungal one.
A single dose of fosfomycin — Single-dose fosfomycin is a cystitis option, not treatment of a febrile kidney infection.
citation: IDSA 2011 guidelines for uncomplicated cystitis and pyelonephritis in women, which remain the IDSA guidance.

examTakeaway: Thrombolysis is not given until blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg. A pressure of 200/120 has to come down first.
scenario: A 66-year-old man was last known well 90 minutes ago. He has aphasia and a right-arm drift. CT shows no hemorrhage. Blood pressure is 200/120 mm Hg. A colleague draws up alteplase and says the clock matters more than the pressure.
question: What has to happen to the pressure before alteplase?
options: Give alteplase now. The window overrides any pressure
Lower it below 185/110 mm Hg first. Do not give the drug at 200/120
Lower the pressure below 120/70 and then wait until the next day
Start heparin instead, because the pressure is high
No treatment of pressure or clot because 90 minutes is too late
correctAnswer: Lower it below 185/110 mm Hg first. Do not give the drug at 200/120
explanation:
Thrombolysis is not given until blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg. A pressure of 200/120 has to come down first. Ninety minutes is still inside the window, so the pressure is treated and the drug is not given at this number. 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke, which remain the AHA/ASA source for the blood-pressure limit before thrombolysis and for antiplatelet timing.

Lower it below 185/110 mm Hg first. Do not give the drug at 200/120
Give alteplase now. The window overrides any pressure — The pressure limit is a condition of giving the drug, not a detail the clock erases.
Lower the pressure below 120/70 and then wait until the next day — The target before treatment is below 185/110, not below 120, and the window should not be spent waiting until tomorrow.
Start heparin instead, because the pressure is high — Heparin is not the substitute for a patient who may still receive thrombolysis.
No treatment of pressure or clot because 90 minutes is too late — Ninety minutes is early. The barrier is the pressure, not the clock.
citation: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke, which remain the AHA/ASA source for the blood-pressure limit before thrombolysis and for antiplatelet timing.

examTakeaway: Aspirin is given after ischemic stroke, but not within 24 hours of thrombolysis.
scenario: A 71-year-old woman received alteplase two hours ago for an ischemic stroke. She is stable. A colleague orders aspirin 325 mg now and says every stroke gets aspirin in the first hour regardless of thrombolysis.
question: When can aspirin be given?
options: Immediately, because thrombolysis does not change antiplatelet timing
Never, because a stroke patient cannot take aspirin at any later time
After 24 hours from the alteplase, not at the two-hour mark
Heparin infusion starting now, with aspirin
Aspirin only if a second CT shows hemorrhage
correctAnswer: After 24 hours from the alteplase, not at the two-hour mark
explanation:
Aspirin is given after ischemic stroke, but not within 24 hours of thrombolysis. Two hours is inside that exclusion. Giving it now adds bleeding without a guideline indication. 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke, which remain the AHA/ASA source for the blood-pressure limit before thrombolysis and for antiplatelet timing.

After 24 hours from the alteplase, not at the two-hour mark
Immediately, because thrombolysis does not change antiplatelet timing — Thrombolysis is exactly what delays aspirin for 24 hours.
Never, because a stroke patient cannot take aspirin at any later time — Aspirin is used after the 24-hour window. It is not banned forever.
Heparin infusion starting now, with aspirin — Routine anticoagulation is not the acute treatment, and aspirin is still too early.
Aspirin only if a second CT shows hemorrhage — Hemorrhage would be a reason to avoid aspirin. A stable patient still waits 24 hours, then gets aspirin if imaging allows.
citation: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke, which remain the AHA/ASA source for the blood-pressure limit before thrombolysis and for antiplatelet timing.

examTakeaway: Convulsive status epilepticus is treated first with a benzodiazepine, not with phenytoin as the opening drug.
scenario: A 23-year-old man has been convulsing for 6 minutes. He is still seizing. Glucose is 110 mg/dL and the airway is supported. A colleague skips a benzodiazepine and loads phenytoin because a longer-acting drug should come first.
question: Which drug is given first?
options: Phenytoin first, with no benzodiazepine
Oral carbamazepine tablets while he is convulsing
Observation until the seizure reaches 30 minutes
A benzodiazepine, such as intravenous lorazepam or intramuscular midazolam
Antibiotics before any antiseizure drug
correctAnswer: A benzodiazepine, such as intravenous lorazepam or intramuscular midazolam
explanation:
Convulsive status epilepticus is treated first with a benzodiazepine, not with phenytoin as the opening drug. Six minutes of convulsions is already status. The benzodiazepine is the emergent drug. A longer-acting antiseizure drug comes if seizures continue. American Epilepsy Society guideline for convulsive status epilepticus, 2016.

A benzodiazepine, such as intravenous lorazepam or intramuscular midazolam
Phenytoin first, with no benzodiazepine — Phenytoin is not the emergent first drug.
Oral carbamazepine tablets while he is convulsing — An oral tablet is not an emergent route.
Observation until the seizure reaches 30 minutes — Treatment starts at about 5 minutes, not at 30.
Antibiotics before any antiseizure drug — There is no finding that makes infection the first drug.
citation: American Epilepsy Society guideline for convulsive status epilepticus, 2016.

examTakeaway: Benzodiazepines are not used for posttraumatic stress disorder. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the preferred treatment.
scenario: A 35-year-old woman has nightmares, avoidance, and hyperarousal three months after an assault. She is not in alcohol withdrawal. A colleague starts diazepam daily and says psychotherapy can wait until the benzodiazepine fails.
question: Why is daily diazepam the wrong treatment?
options: Diazepam is first-line because nightmares are a sleep disorder only
No treatment until symptoms have lasted two years
An antipsychotic as the required first drug
Daily alcohol as a safer substitute for diazepam
Benzodiazepines are recommended against. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the preferred treatment
correctAnswer: Benzodiazepines are recommended against. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the preferred treatment
explanation:
Benzodiazepines are not used for posttraumatic stress disorder. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the preferred treatment. She is not withdrawing from alcohol, so a benzodiazepine is not filling some other indication. An SSRI can be discussed. Diazepam is not the plan. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, 2023.

Benzodiazepines are recommended against. Trauma-focused psychotherapy is the preferred treatment
Diazepam is first-line because nightmares are a sleep disorder only — Nightmares in this pattern are part of the stress disorder, not a reason for a benzodiazepine.
No treatment until symptoms have lasted two years — Three months is already long enough to treat.
An antipsychotic as the required first drug — An antipsychotic is not the preferred first treatment.
Daily alcohol as a safer substitute for diazepam — Alcohol is not a treatment for this disorder.
citation: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, 2023.

examTakeaway: Major depression is treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant such as an SSRI. A benzodiazepine is not the antidepressant.
scenario: A 42-year-old man has had low mood, poor sleep, and loss of interest for six weeks. He is not manic and not withdrawing from alcohol. A colleague prescribes alprazolam three times a day and no antidepressant.
question: Why does alprazolam miss the diagnosis?
options: It is not an antidepressant. Depression is treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant
Alprazolam is the preferred antidepressant
No treatment until symptoms last a year
Lithium monotherapy as the required first drug for every low mood
Two antidepressants plus a benzodiazepine on day 1
correctAnswer: It is not an antidepressant. Depression is treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant
explanation:
Major depression is treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant such as an SSRI. A benzodiazepine is not the antidepressant. Six weeks of low mood and anhedonia is a depressive episode. Alprazolam does not treat that illness. VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Major Depressive Disorder, 2022.

It is not an antidepressant. Depression is treated with psychotherapy or an antidepressant
Alprazolam is the preferred antidepressant — It is a benzodiazepine, not an antidepressant.
No treatment until symptoms last a year — Six weeks is enough to treat.
Lithium monotherapy as the required first drug for every low mood — Lithium is not the first drug of ordinary unipolar depression.
Two antidepressants plus a benzodiazepine on day 1 — Starting two antidepressants and a benzodiazepine together is not the initial plan.
citation: VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Major Depressive Disorder, 2022.

examTakeaway: Bipolar depression is not treated with antidepressant monotherapy. A mood stabilizer or an approved bipolar regimen is used.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman has bipolar I disorder and is now depressed. She is not manic today. A colleague starts sertraline alone and stops her mood stabilizer, saying depression is always treated with an antidepressant by itself.
question: Why is sertraline alone the wrong change?
options: Sertraline alone is the standard bipolar depression regimen
Antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize bipolar illness. Keep a mood stabilizer in the regimen
Stop every drug until the next mania
Add two antidepressants and no mood stabilizer
Daily diazepam as the mood stabilizer
correctAnswer: Antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize bipolar illness. Keep a mood stabilizer in the regimen
explanation:
Bipolar depression is not treated with antidepressant monotherapy. A mood stabilizer or an approved bipolar regimen is used. Stopping the mood stabilizer and leaving sertraline alone is the error. CANMAT and ISBD 2018 guidelines for the management of patients with bipolar disorder.

Antidepressant monotherapy can destabilize bipolar illness. Keep a mood stabilizer in the regimen
Sertraline alone is the standard bipolar depression regimen — Monotherapy with an antidepressant is what the guidelines advise against.
Stop every drug until the next mania — Depression is treated. Waiting for mania is not the plan.
Add two antidepressants and no mood stabilizer — More antidepressant monotherapy is still the wrong structure.
Daily diazepam as the mood stabilizer — A benzodiazepine is not a mood stabilizer.
citation: CANMAT and ISBD 2018 guidelines for the management of patients with bipolar disorder.

examTakeaway: Schizophrenia is started on one antipsychotic. Two antipsychotics are not begun together.
scenario: A 24-year-old man has a first episode of psychosis. He has hallucinations and disorganization for six weeks. Medical causes have been excluded. A colleague starts haloperidol and olanzapine together on day 1.
question: How many antipsychotics are started?
options: Two, because a first episode needs dual therapy
None, until he has been psychotic for a year
One. A second antipsychotic is not added at the start
A benzodiazepine only, with no antipsychotic
Clozapine as the required first drug before any other antipsychotic
correctAnswer: One. A second antipsychotic is not added at the start
explanation:
Schizophrenia is started on one antipsychotic. Two antipsychotics are not begun together. He needs treatment, and the treatment is monotherapy. A second drug is not the way to make the first day stronger. APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 2020.

One. A second antipsychotic is not added at the start
Two, because a first episode needs dual therapy — The guideline recommends against starting two.
None, until he has been psychotic for a year — Six weeks of psychosis is treated.
A benzodiazepine only, with no antipsychotic — A benzodiazepine does not treat the psychotic illness.
Clozapine as the required first drug before any other antipsychotic — Clozapine is reserved for treatment resistance, not the first prescription.
citation: APA Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Schizophrenia, 2020.

examTakeaway: Naltrexone helps alcohol use disorder only when the patient is not taking an opioid. An opioid use history that is current makes naltrexone the wrong drug.
scenario: A 48-year-old man wants help stopping alcohol. He takes methadone for opioid use disorder and is not in alcohol withdrawal today. His liver enzymes are twice normal. A colleague prescribes naltrexone and says methadone does not interact with it.
question: Why is naltrexone unsafe with his methadone?
options: Naltrexone is required precisely because he takes methadone
Naltrexone treats alcohol withdrawal tremors
Disulfiram is mandatory before any other drug can be considered
Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors and can precipitate withdrawal from methadone
No medication exists for alcohol use disorder
correctAnswer: Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors and can precipitate withdrawal from methadone
explanation:
Naltrexone helps alcohol use disorder only when the patient is not taking an opioid. An opioid use history that is current makes naltrexone the wrong drug. He is on methadone. Acamprosate can be discussed. Naltrexone cannot. APA Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder, 2018.

Naltrexone blocks opioid receptors and can precipitate withdrawal from methadone
Naltrexone is required precisely because he takes methadone — Methadone is the contraindication, not the indication.
Naltrexone treats alcohol withdrawal tremors — He is not in withdrawal, and naltrexone is not the withdrawal drug.
Disulfiram is mandatory before any other drug can be considered — Disulfiram is not a required first step.
No medication exists for alcohol use disorder — Effective medications exist. This one is simply the wrong choice on methadone.
citation: APA Practice Guideline for the Pharmacological Treatment of Patients With Alcohol Use Disorder, 2018.

examTakeaway: Alcohol withdrawal is treated with a benzodiazepine. An antipsychotic is not the withdrawal drug.
scenario: A 52-year-old woman stopped drinking 18 hours ago. She is tremulous, her pulse is 120/min, and her blood pressure is 160/96 mm Hg. She is oriented and not seizing. A colleague orders haloperidol and no benzodiazepine.
question: Which drug treats this withdrawal?
options: Haloperidol alone
Naltrexone as the acute withdrawal drug
No drug until a seizure occurs
A beta blocker as the only drug
A benzodiazepine, titrated to the signs, not haloperidol as the withdrawal treatment
correctAnswer: A benzodiazepine, titrated to the signs, not haloperidol as the withdrawal treatment
explanation:
Alcohol withdrawal is treated with a benzodiazepine. An antipsychotic is not the withdrawal drug. Her pulse and tremor are withdrawal. Haloperidol can lower the seizure threshold and does not replace the benzodiazepine. ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management, 2020.

A benzodiazepine, titrated to the signs, not haloperidol as the withdrawal treatment
Haloperidol alone — An antipsychotic does not treat the withdrawal syndrome.
Naltrexone as the acute withdrawal drug — Naltrexone is for relapse prevention, not for acute autonomic withdrawal.
No drug until a seizure occurs — Tremor and a pulse of 120 are already enough to treat.
A beta blocker as the only drug — A beta blocker can mask signs. It is not the primary withdrawal treatment.
citation: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management, 2020.
